title: The consecration
hook: the words of Jesus are spoken and Catholics believe bread and wine become his body and blood (CCC 1376)
tomorrow: The Great Amen and the Our Father

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy, the seraphim's song, as heaven and earth sing together. Your line was heaven joins in.

The singing has stopped. In this church, everyone is kneeling, and even the kids have gone quiet. The priest bends over the altar, holding a thin, round piece of bread, and speaks the words Jesus said at the Last Supper. He lifts it high, above his head, so everyone can see. A small bell rings, or a set of bells. He lowers it, and genuflects. Then the same with the cup. For a few seconds, nobody in the room moves. What Catholics believe just happened has a long, strange name.
screen: `THE SINGING STOPS.` → `THE BREAD LIFTED HIGH.` → `A BELL, AND SILENCE.`

segments.voice: At the Last Supper, Luke says, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to his friends, saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Then the cup: his blood, of the new covenant. At the consecration, the priest repeats those words, not as a story about Jesus, but in the first person, as Christ. Catholics believe that at those words, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Not a symbol, not a reminder: Christ himself, really present. The name the Church gave this is transubstantiation. Trans, across. Substance, what a thing most deeply is. The Church teaches that the substance changes completely, while everything you can see, touch or taste stays the same: it still looks like bread, and tastes like wine. No chemistry changes; in Catholic teaching, the whole reality does. That's why the bell, the kneeling, the genuflection after each elevation. Catholics often point to John's Gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this meal in different ways. Orthodox Christians also believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, and usually prefer not to explain how. Lutherans believe Christ is truly present, without this Catholic explanation. Other Protestants speak of a spiritual presence, or of a memorial. For Catholics, it's the center of their worship.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `REALLY PRESENT, NOT A SYMBOL.` · `THE SUBSTANCE CHANGES, NOT THE LOOK.` · `OTHER CHRISTIANS SEE IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, you can kneel; if not, sit with your hands open in your lap. Picture the moment in that church, the bread lifted, the bell, the silence that follows, and don't try to think anything about it; just be as still as that room. If you pray, you can simply be present to the one who, Catholics believe, is present there.
Transubstantiation. The Catholic name for the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance stays the same. Today's word.
Your line: this is my body. Words from the Last Supper, spoken again at the altar. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: During the Eucharistic Prayer the priest speaks Christ's words over the bread and wine, elevates each for the people to see and genuflects; bells are often rung, and in many countries the congregation kneels throughout.

what a scholar hears: used at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, explained by Aquinas with Aristotle's substance and accidents, and defined at Trent (CCC 1376).

chat.says: What does that long word, transubstantiation, actually mean?
options: The bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, though they look the same.
It's the Latin name for the little bell rung when the priest lifts the bread.
The bread begins to look and taste different after the priest's words.
chat.meaning: The Church teaches the substance changes completely into Christ's body and blood, while everything you can see, touch or taste stays the same.

consecration.meaning: when the priest says Jesus's Last Supper words over bread and wine

covenant.meaning: a solemn bond between God and people

Lutherans.meaning: Christians who believe Christ is truly present, without this explanation

notes: Douay-Rheims Luke 22:19 and John 6:56 given from memory; confirm wording and verse numbering.
CCC 1376 (quoting Trent) is paraphrased, not quoted; the Catechism's English translation is copyrighted.
'In the first person, as Christ' refers to the priest acting in persona Christi (CCC 1548). Confirm.

Other traditions described without ranking: Orthodox (real change, reluctance to define the manner), Lutheran (real presence without transubstantiation), many Protestants (memorial or spiritual presence). A Keeper and an ecumenical reviewer should check fairness.
Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used 'transsubstantiatis'; Trent defined 'transubstantiation' as 'fitting and proper'. Confirm the trapdoor.
Bells at the elevation are customary, not required; kneeling posture varies by country. Confirm.
